lessons.title: Multiplication as Repeated Addition & Arrays
lessons.description: Understand multiplication as adding the same number many times. Use arrays (rows and columns of dots) to visualize it!
lessons.formula:
Multiplication as Repeated Addition:

3 × 4 = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
(3 groups of 4)

Arrays:
3 rows × 4 columns = 12 dots
• • • •
• • • •
• • • •

3 × 4 = 12 (read as "3 times 4 equals 12")
lessons.content:
Multiplication is a fast way of adding the same number over and over. Instead of writing 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, you write 3 × 4 = 12. The "3" tells you how many groups, and the "4" tells you how many in each group. The numbers you multiply are called factors, and the answer is called the product.

An array is a picture that shows multiplication using rows and columns of dots. A 3 × 4 array has 3 rows with 4 dots in each row, totaling 12 dots. Arrays help you see that 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 give the same answer (12) — even though the arrangement looks different! This is the commutative property.

Arrays are everywhere in real life: egg cartons (2 × 6), ice cube trays, bookshelves with rows of books, and windows with panes. Every rectangular arrangement is an array!
steps: Identify the number of groups (first factor) and the size of each group (second factor)
Write it as repeated addition: e.g., 3 × 4 = 4 + 4 + 4
Add all the groups together to find the product: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
Draw an array to match: rows = first factor, columns = second factor
Remember: switching the factors gives the same product (commutative property)

examples.title: Repeated Addition to Multiplication
examples.text:
5 × 3 means 5 groups of 3:

3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15

As an array (5 rows, 3 columns):
• • •
• • •
• • •
• • •
• • •

5 × 3 = 15 and 3 × 5 = 15 (same answer!)

examples.title: Real-World Arrays
examples.text:
An egg carton has 2 rows of 6 eggs.

Array: 2 × 6 = 12 eggs
Repeated addition: 6 + 6 = 12

A muffin pan has 3 rows of 4 cups:
3 × 4 = 12 muffin cups

lessons.tip: Draw arrays on graph paper or use small objects (buttons, beans, coins) to build arrays physically. This hands-on practice helps your brain connect the visual picture to the multiplication fact. Once the picture is in your mind, recalling facts becomes automatic!

quiz.q: What is 4 × 5 as repeated addition?
quiz.explanation: 4 × 5 means 4 groups of 5, written as 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20. Note: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 20 also works — that's 5 × 4!

quiz.q: An array has 3 rows with 6 dots in each row. What multiplication fact does it show?
quiz.explanation: 3 rows × 6 columns = 3 × 6 = 18 dots total.

quiz.q: Which shows the commutative property of multiplication?
quiz.explanation: The commutative property states that switching the order of factors doesn't change the product: 3 × 4 = 4 × 3.

lessons.title: Times Tables Fluency (1-10)
lessons.description: Master all multiplication facts from ×1 to ×10 with helpful patterns, tricks, and strategies!
lessons.formula:
Times Tables Quick Reference:

×1: Any number × 1 = itself (7 × 1 = 7)
×2: Doubles! (2 × 6 = 12, same as 6 + 6)
×3: Skip count by 3s
×4: Double, then double again (3 × 4 = 3×2×2 = 12)
×5: Ends in 0 or 5 (5, 10, 15, 20...)
×6: ×5 plus one more group
×9: Finger trick or digit sum = 9
×10: Add a zero! (7 × 10 = 70)
lessons.content:
Knowing your times tables from ×1 to ×10 by heart is one of the most important skills in all of math. It makes multiplication, division, fractions, and algebra SO much easier! The good news is that each table has patterns and tricks to help you learn them faster.

Easy tables first: The ×1 table is trivial (any number times 1 is itself). The ×2 table is just doubles (2 × 7 = 14 is the same as 7 + 7). The ×5 table follows a simple pattern: every answer ends in 0 or 5. The ×10 table is the easiest — just add a zero to the other number!

Trickier tables: For ×4, double the number and then double again (3 × 4 = 3 doubled is 6, doubled again is 12). For ×9, use the famous finger trick: hold up all 10 fingers, put down the finger for the number you're multiplying by, and the remaining fingers give you the answer! For ×6, think of ×5 plus one more group (6 × 7 = 5 × 7 + 7 = 35 + 7 = 42).
steps: Start with the easiest tables: ×1, ×2, ×5, and ×10 — learn these perfectly first
Practice ×3 and ×4 using skip counting and doubling tricks
Learn ×6 by relating it to ×5 (add one more group)
Master ×9 using the finger trick or the digit-sum pattern
Learn ×7 and ×8 last — these are the hardest, use flashcards and games
Practice mixed facts daily with speed drills until each answer comes in under 3 seconds

examples.title: ×9 Finger Trick
examples.text:
To find 9 × 4:

Hold up 10 fingers. Put down your 4th finger (left index).
Fingers before: 3 (hundreds/tens digit)
Fingers after: 6 (ones digit)
Answer: 36!

Check: 9 × 4 = 36 ✓

examples.title: ×4 Doubling Strategy
examples.text:
Find 6 × 4:

Step 1: Double 6 = 12
Step 2: Double 12 = 24

Answer: 6 × 4 = 24

Another: 7 × 4 → 7 doubled = 14 → 14 doubled = 28

lessons.tip: Create a multiplication chart and color in the facts you've mastered. Celebrate when a whole row is done! Use apps, flashcards, and speed games to practice daily. Aim for 3 seconds or less per fact. The ×7 and ×8 facts are the last to master — for 7 × 8 = 56, remember: "5, 6, 7, 8" → 56 = 7 × 8!

quiz.q: What is 7 × 8?
quiz.explanation: 7 × 8 = 56. Remember the trick: 5, 6, 7, 8 → 56 = 7 × 8!

quiz.q: Using the ×9 finger trick, what is 9 × 3?
quiz.explanation: Put down your 3rd finger. Fingers before: 2. Fingers after: 7. Answer: 27. Also: 2 + 7 = 9 (digit sum pattern for ×9)!

quiz.q: What pattern does the ×5 table follow?
quiz.explanation: The ×5 table always produces numbers ending in 0 or 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30...

lessons.title: Multiplication & Division Facts
lessons.description: Memorize multiplication and division facts up to 10×10 and understand the relationship!
lessons.formula:
Multiplication & Division are inverse:
3 × 4 = 12  and  12 ÷ 3 = 4
12 ÷ 4 = 3  and  4 × 3 = 12
lessons.content:
Multiplication and division are inverse operations — they undo each other! If you know that 6 × 7 = 42, then you also know 42 ÷ 6 = 7 and 42 ÷ 7 = 6. These four facts form a fact family.

By 3rd grade, you should know all your multiplication facts from 0 × 0 up to 10 × 10. Practice with flashcards, songs, and games. The more you practice, the faster you'll recall them!

Division is asking 'how many times does this number go into that number?' or 'if we split this into equal groups, how many in each?' For 24 ÷ 6, you're asking: how many groups of 6 make 24?
steps: Study one multiplication table at a time (start with ×2, ×5, ×10)
Practice the related division facts at the same time
Use arrays and groups to visualize facts
Play games and use flashcards for speed practice
Learn tricks: ×9 — hold up 10 fingers, fold down the 3rd finger = 27!

examples.title: Fact Family: 4, 7, 28
examples.text: 4 × 7 = 28, 7 × 4 = 28, 28 ÷ 4 = 7, 28 ÷ 7 = 4. All four facts are connected!

examples.title: Division: 36 ÷ 9
examples.text: Think: 9 × ? = 36. Since 9 × 4 = 36, the answer is 36 ÷ 9 = 4.

lessons.tip: Learn your ×9 facts with the hand trick! Hold up both hands, fold down the finger for the number you're multiplying by 9. The fingers to the left = tens digit, fingers to the right = ones digit. For 9 × 4, fold the 4th finger: 3 fingers left, 6 fingers right = 36!

quiz.q: What is 7 × 8?
quiz.explanation: 7 × 8 = 56. A helpful mnemonic: '7 × 8 = 56 (5, 6, 7, 8 — count up!)'

quiz.q: What is 48 ÷ 6?
Which is the fact family for 3, 9, 27?
quiz.explanation: A multiplication/division fact family connects 3 numbers with × and ÷.

quiz.q: What is 9 × 9?

lessons.title: Multiplication Strategies
lessons.description: Use arrays, equal groups, repeated addition, and properties to solve multiplication problems within 100.
lessons.formula:
Multiplication Properties:
Commutative: 3 x 4 = 4 x 3 = 12
Zero Property: 5 x 0 = 0
Identity: 7 x 1 = 7
Repeated Addition: 3 x 4 = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
lessons.content:
There are many strategies to solve multiplication problems. An array is a rectangular arrangement of objects in rows and columns. If you have 3 rows of 4 dots, that's 3 x 4 = 12. You can also think of multiplication as equal groups: 4 bags with 3 apples each means 4 x 3 = 12.

The commutative property says you can flip the numbers: 3 x 4 gives the same answer as 4 x 3. This means you can always choose the easier order to multiply! The zero property tells us any number times zero is zero, and the identity property says any number times one is itself.
steps: Identify the two numbers being multiplied (factors)
Choose a strategy: draw an array, make equal groups, or use repeated addition
Use the commutative property to flip the numbers if it makes the problem easier
Count the total to find the product
Check: does your answer make sense? Estimate first if needed

examples.title: Array: 4 Rows of 5
examples.text: Draw 4 rows with 5 stars in each row: * * * * * / * * * * * / * * * * * / * * * * *. Count all 20 stars. So 4 x 5 = 20.

examples.title: Commutative Property: 7 x 3
examples.text: 7 x 3 is the same as 3 x 7. Since 3 x 7 = 21 is easier for some students, you can flip it! Both equal 21.

lessons.tip: When you memorize a fact like 6 x 8 = 48, you automatically know 8 x 6 = 48 too! That is the commutative property cutting your work in half. Every multiplication fact you learn is really TWO facts.

quiz.q: What is 5 x 6 using equal groups?
Which property says 3 x 7 = 7 x 3?
quiz.explanation: The Commutative Property says you can flip the order of the factors and get the same product.

quiz.q: What is 9 x 0?
quiz.explanation: The Zero Property: any number multiplied by 0 equals 0.

lessons.title: Division Strategies
lessons.description: Understand division as sharing equally and as repeated subtraction, and use fact families.
lessons.formula:
Division as Sharing:
12 ÷ 3 = 4 means split 12 into 3 equal groups of 4

Division as Repeated Subtraction:
12 - 3 - 3 - 3 - 3 = 0 (subtracted 4 times)
So 12 ÷ 3 = 4

Fact Family: 3 x 4 = 12, 12 ÷ 3 = 4, 12 ÷ 4 = 3
lessons.content:
Division is the opposite of multiplication. There are two main ways to think about it. Sharing means dividing a total into equal groups: 12 cookies shared among 3 friends means each friend gets 4 cookies (12 ÷ 3 = 4). Repeated subtraction means subtracting the same number until you reach zero: starting at 12, subtract 3 four times to reach 0, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4.

Every multiplication fact has a division fact family. If you know 4 x 6 = 24, then you also know 24 ÷ 4 = 6 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Learning your multiplication facts automatically gives you division facts too!
steps: Identify the total (dividend) and the number you are dividing by (divisor)
Think: how many groups? OR how many in each group?
Use repeated subtraction or think of the related multiplication fact
Write the division equation: dividend ÷ divisor = quotient
Check: multiply quotient x divisor. It should equal the dividend

examples.title: Sharing: 20 ÷ 4
examples.text: You have 20 stickers and want to share them equally among 4 friends. Each friend gets 5 stickers. 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Check: 5 x 4 = 20.

examples.title: Repeated Subtraction: 15 ÷ 5
examples.text: Start at 15. Subtract 5: 15 - 5 = 10. Subtract 5: 10 - 5 = 5. Subtract 5: 5 - 5 = 0. You subtracted 5 three times. So 15 ÷ 5 = 3.

lessons.tip: If you get stuck on a division problem, flip it into multiplication! For 24 ÷ 6, think: 6 times what equals 24? Since 6 x 4 = 24, the answer is 4. Multiplication is your best division tool!

quiz.q: What is 18 ÷ 2?
Which multiplication fact helps you solve 28 ÷ 4?
You have 24 cookies and put them in bags of 6. How many bags?
quiz.explanation: 24 ÷ 6 = 4. You can fill 4 bags.

lessons.title: Properties of Multiplication
lessons.description: Learn the commutative, associative, and distributive properties that make multiplication easier!
lessons.formula:
Commutative: 3 x 4 = 4 x 3 (order doesn't matter)
Associative: (2 x 3) x 4 = 2 x (3 x 4)
Distributive: 5 x 7 = 5 x (5 + 2) = 25 + 10 = 35
lessons.content:
Multiplication has three special properties that always work. The commutative property says order does not matter: 3 x 4 = 12 and 4 x 3 = 12. If you know 7 x 8 = 56, you also know 8 x 7 = 56. This means you only need to memorize each fact once!

The associative property says grouping does not matter when multiplying three or more numbers. (2 x 3) x 4 = 6 x 4 = 24, and 2 x (3 x 4) = 2 x 12 = 24. Group the easiest pair first to save time!

The distributive property lets you break apart a factor into friendlier numbers. For 6 x 7, think of 7 as 5 + 2: 6 x 5 = 30, 6 x 2 = 12, total = 42. This property connects multiplication to addition and is used throughout all of algebra!
steps: Commutative: flip the order, same answer (3x4 = 4x3)
Associative: group any way you like (2x3)x4 = 2x(3x4)
Distributive: break one factor into parts (8x7 = 8x5 + 8x2)
Practice each property with different numbers
Use distributive for hard facts you have not memorized yet

examples.title: Commutative Property
examples.text: 5 x 9 = 45 and 9 x 5 = 45. Same answer either way! You only need to memorize once.

examples.title: Distributive Property
examples.text: 8 x 7: Break 7 into 5+2. 8x5=40, 8x2=16, 40+16=56. Hard fact made easy!

lessons.tip: The distributive property is your best friend for hard facts! Forget 7x8? Use 7x(10-2) = 70-14 = 56.

quiz.q: Which property says 4 x 7 = 7 x 4?
quiz.explanation: Commutative: flip the order of factors, same product.

quiz.q: Use distributive: 9 x 6 = 9 x (5 + ?)
quiz.explanation: Break 6 into 5+1: 9x5=45, 9x1=9, total=54.

quiz.q: (3 x 4) x 2 = 3 x (4 x 2) uses which property?
quiz.explanation: Associative: changing grouping does not change the product.

lessons.title: Rounding to the Nearest 10 and 100
lessons.description: Round numbers to the nearest ten or hundred for quick estimation!
lessons.formula:
Round to 10: look at ONES digit
0-4 round down, 5-9 round up
47 -> 50, 43 -> 40

Round to 100: look at TENS digit
372 -> 400, 328 -> 300
lessons.content:
Rounding to the nearest ten or hundred helps you estimate answers quickly. When rounding to the nearest ten, look at the ones digit. When rounding to the nearest hundred, look at the tens digit. The rule is always the same: 0-4 rounds down, 5-9 rounds up!

For example, 342 rounded to the nearest hundred: the tens digit is 4 (less than 5), so round down to 300. But 367 has a tens digit of 6 (5 or more), so round up to 400. Think of it as asking: is this number closer to 300 or 400?

Estimation is used everywhere in real life. Adding 285 + 413? Round each to the nearest hundred: 300 + 400 = 700. The exact answer is 698, very close to 700! Always estimate before calculating to catch mistakes.
steps: Decide: nearest 10 or nearest 100?
Look at the digit one place to the RIGHT of your target
0-4: keep the target, make everything right of it zero
5-9: add 1 to the target, make everything right of it zero
Check: is the rounded number close to the original?

examples.title: Rounding to Hundred
examples.text: 567: tens digit is 7 (5+), round up to 600. 523: tens digit is 2 (less than 5), round down to 500.

examples.title: Estimating a Sum
examples.text: 347 + 289: Round to nearest 100: 300 + 300 = 600. Exact is 636. Estimate is reasonable!

lessons.tip: Five is the tipping point! Think of 5 as the mountain peak: 0-4 roll down (round down), 5-9 roll up (round up).

quiz.q: Round 378 to nearest hundred.
quiz.explanation: Tens digit is 7 (5+), round up to 400.

quiz.q: Round 145 to nearest ten.
quiz.explanation: Ones digit is 5, round up to 150.

quiz.q: Estimate 623 + 189 (nearest hundred).
What rounds to 500?
quiz.explanation: 451: tens digit is 5, round up to 500.

lessons.title: Division as Equal Sharing and Grouping
lessons.description: Understand division by sharing equally among groups or making equal-sized groups!
lessons.formula:
Sharing: 24 / 6 = 4 each (6 groups, find size)
Grouping: 24 / 6 = 4 groups (size 6, find count)

Dividend / Divisor = Quotient
lessons.content:
There are two ways to think about division! Sharing means dividing a total into a known number of groups to find how many each gets. Example: 24 cookies among 6 friends = 4 each. Grouping means dividing into groups of a known size to find how many groups. Example: 24 cookies in bags of 6 = 4 bags.

Both use the same equation (24 / 6 = 4) but the thinking differs. In sharing, you know the number OF groups and find the SIZE. In grouping, you know the SIZE of groups and find the NUMBER of groups.

Sometimes division leaves a remainder. 17 cookies among 5 friends: each gets 3 with 2 left over. We write 17 / 5 = 3 R 2. Remainders happen in real life all the time!
steps: Read: what is the total (dividend)?
Identify: sharing (find size) or grouping (find count)?
Sharing: total / number of groups = size of each
Grouping: total / group size = number of groups
Check: quotient x divisor should be close to dividend

examples.title: Sharing Model
examples.text: 18 pencils / 3 students = 6 pencils each. You knew 3 groups, found size 6.

examples.title: Grouping Model
examples.text: 20 books on shelves of 4 = 5 shelves. You knew size 4, found count 5.

lessons.tip: Use 24 counters. Share among 6 plates (sharing), then make groups of 6 (grouping). Feel the difference!

quiz.q: 32 / 8 = ? (sharing model)
quiz.explanation: 32 / 8 = 4. Each gets 4.

quiz.q: 28 books in stacks of 7 = ? (grouping)
quiz.explanation: 28 / 7 = 4 stacks.
4x6=24, remainder 1. Answer: 6 R 1.

quiz.q: Which is grouping?
quiz.explanation: Grouping: know size (5 per bag), find number of groups.

lessons.title: Perimeter of Polygons
lessons.description: Find the distance around any shape by adding all its side lengths!
lessons.formula:
Perimeter = sum of ALL sides
Rectangle: P = 2(L + W)
Square: P = 4 x s
Triangle: P = a + b + c
lessons.content:
Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a shape. Imagine walking along every edge and back to start — that distance is the perimeter! Simply add up all side lengths.

For a rectangle with length 8 and width 5: P = 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26. Since rectangles have two pairs of equal sides, use the shortcut P = 2(L + W) = 2(8 + 5) = 26. For a square with side 6: all sides equal, so P = 4 x 6 = 24.

Perimeter is used in real life for fencing, baseboards, picture frames, and borders. For any shape, even irregular ones, just add every side length. The rule never changes!
steps: Identify the shape and find every side length
Add ALL side lengths together
For rectangles: use P = 2(L + W)
For squares: use P = 4 x s
Always include units (cm, m, in, ft)

examples.title: Rectangle Perimeter
examples.text: Garden 12m x 8m: P = 2(12+8) = 40m of fencing needed!

lessons.tip: Perimeter has RIM in it — like the outer rim of a shape! Add all the outer edges.

quiz.q: Rectangle 9cm x 4cm. Perimeter?
Square side 7in. Perimeter?
quiz.explanation: P = 4 x 7 = 28 inches.

quiz.q: Triangle sides 6, 8, 10cm. Perimeter?
Fence for 15m x 10m yard?

lessons.title: Multiplying Multiples of 10
lessons.description: Multiply numbers like 30 x 40 using place value shortcuts!
lessons.formula:
3 x 4 = 12
30 x 4 = 120
30 x 40 = 1,200

Multiply non-zero digits, then add ALL the zeros!
lessons.content:
When multiplying numbers ending in zero, there is a powerful shortcut! Ignore the zeros, multiply the non-zero digits, then add back all the zeros. For 30 x 40: 3 x 4 = 12, then add two zeros: 1,200!

This works because each zero represents a power of ten. 30 is '3 tens' and 40 is '4 tens'. Multiply them: 3 tens x 4 tens = 12 hundreds = 1,200. The zeros just get added together!

It works for any combination: 500 x 60 = 5 x 6 = 30, add three zeros = 30,000. 200 x 300 = 2 x 3 = 6, add four zeros = 60,000. Count zeros first so you do not forget any!
steps: Count total zeros in both factors
Multiply only the non-zero digits
Append all the zeros to the product
lessons.tip: Count zeros BEFORE multiplying. 200x500: three zeros total (2+1). Never forget a zero!

quiz.explanation: 4x3=12, two zeros = 1,200.
2x5=10, three zeros = 10,000.
6x8=48, one zero = 480.

quiz.q: Zeros in answer to 300 x 400?
quiz.explanation: Two from 300 + two from 400 = four zeros.

lessons.title: Fractions on a Number Line
lessons.description: Plot and identify fractions on a number line from 0 to 1!
lessons.formula:
To place a fraction on a number line:
1. Divide the segment from 0 to 1 into equal parts
2. Count the parts from 0
3/4 means: divide into 4 parts, go to the 3rd
lessons.content:
A number line is a straight line with numbers placed at equal distances. Between 0 and 1, fractions live! To place a fraction like 3/4 on a number line, first divide the space between 0 and 1 into 4 equal sections. Then count 3 of those sections from 0.

Each fraction's denominator tells you how many equal pieces to divide the number line into, and the numerator tells you how many pieces to count from zero.

Equivalent fractions like 2/4 and 1/2 land on the SAME SPOT on the number line! This is a powerful visual proof that these fractions are equal.
steps: Draw a line and mark 0 on the left and 1 on the right
Look at the denominator: divide the space into that many equal parts
Mark each division with a small tick mark
Count from 0 the number shown by the numerator
Place a dot and label it with the fraction

examples.title: Plotting 2/3
examples.text: Divide between 0 and 1 into 3 equal parts. Count 2 parts from 0. Place a dot at the 2nd mark and label it 2/3.

examples.title: Equivalent Fractions on Number Line
examples.text: Plot 1/2 by dividing into 2 parts. Plot 2/4 by dividing into 4 parts. They land at the same point! 1/2 = 2/4.

lessons.tip: Fractions closer to 1 on the number line are LARGER, and fractions closer to 0 are SMALLER. If one fraction's dot is further to the right, it's the bigger fraction!

quiz.q: On a number line from 0 to 1 divided into 5 parts, which mark represents 3/5?
quiz.explanation: 3/5 means count 3 marks from 0, so it's the 3rd tick mark.

quiz.q: True or False: 1/2 and 2/4 are at the same point on a number line.
quiz.explanation: Yes! 1/2 = 2/4 = 0.5. They're equivalent fractions at the same point.

quiz.q: Which fraction is between 0 and 1/2?
quiz.explanation: 1/4 is at the first quarter mark, which is between 0 and 1/2 (the middle).

quiz.q: If a number line from 0 to 1 has 6 equal marks, what fraction is at the 4th mark?
quiz.explanation: 6 marks means 6ths. The 4th mark from 0 is 4/6.

lessons.title: Equivalent Fractions
lessons.description: Find fractions that name the same amount using models and number lines.
lessons.formula:
Equivalent Fractions:
1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8

Multiply top and bottom by the same number:
1/2 x 2/2 = 2/4
1/2 x 3/3 = 3/6

The value stays the same!
lessons.content:
Equivalent fractions are fractions that look different but represent the same amount. For example, 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent because they cover the same portion of a whole. If you shade half of a rectangle, and then cut each half into 2 smaller pieces, you have 2 out of 4 pieces shaded — that is 2/4, which equals 1/2.

You can find equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing both the numerator and denominator by the same number. This is like cutting each piece into smaller, equal pieces. On a number line, equivalent fractions land on the exact same spot, which is great visual proof!
steps: Start with a fraction you want to find equivalents for
Choose a number to multiply (or divide) both numerator and denominator by
Multiply the top and bottom by the same number
Check with a model: do both fractions cover the same area?
Use a number line to confirm both fractions are at the same point

examples.title: Finding Equivalents of 1/3
examples.text: 1/3 x 2/2 = 2/6. 1/3 x 3/3 = 3/9. So 1/3 = 2/6 = 3/9. All three fractions mark the same point on a number line!

examples.title: Using a Model
examples.text: Draw a bar and shade 2 out of 4 sections. Draw another bar the same size and shade 1 out of 2 sections. They look the same! 2/4 = 1/2.

lessons.tip: If two fractions have the same numerator or denominator, they are NOT automatically equivalent. 2/3 and 2/5 are different because the pieces are different sizes. Always check that you multiplied BOTH top and bottom by the same number!

quiz.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/4?
quiz.explanation: 1/4 x 2/2 = 2/8. Both top and bottom were multiplied by 2.

quiz.q: Are 3/6 and 1/2 equivalent?
quiz.explanation: 3/6 simplifies to 1/2 (divide both by 3). They represent the same amount.

quiz.q: What is 2/3 equivalent to when multiplied by 4?
quiz.explanation: 2/3 x 4/4 = 8/12. Both numerator and denominator are multiplied by 4.

lessons.title: Comparing Fractions
lessons.description: Compare fractions with same numerator or same denominator using models.
lessons.formula:
Same Denominator:
Compare numerators: 2/5 < 4/5
Bigger numerator = bigger fraction

Same Numerator:
Compare denominators: 3/4 > 3/8
Smaller denominator = bigger fraction (fewer, bigger pieces)

Benchmark: 1/2
  2/5 < 1/2,  3/4 > 1/2
lessons.content:
Comparing fractions means figuring out which fraction is bigger. When two fractions have the same denominator, just compare the numerators. For example, 3/8 vs 5/8: since 5 > 3, we know 5/8 > 3/8. Think of it as having 5 slices of pizza vs 3 slices — more slices is more pizza!

When two fractions have the same numerator but different denominators, the rule flips! A smaller denominator means bigger pieces. So 2/3 > 2/5 because thirds are bigger than fifths. You can also use benchmark fractions like 1/2 to help: is the fraction more or less than half?
steps: Look at the denominators: are they the same?
If same denominator: compare the numerators (bigger numerator = bigger fraction)
If same numerator: compare the denominators (smaller denominator = bigger fraction)
If both are different: compare each to a benchmark like 1/2
Draw models (bars or circles) to double-check visually

examples.title: Same Denominator: 4/6 vs 1/6
examples.text: Both have denominator 6. Compare numerators: 4 > 1. So 4/6 > 1/6. Four slices is more than one slice!

examples.title: Same Numerator: 5/8 vs 5/6
examples.text: Both have numerator 5. Compare denominators: 6 < 8. Smaller denominator means bigger pieces, so 5/6 > 5/8.

lessons.tip: Use the "benchmark of 1/2" trick! If a fraction's numerator is more than half its denominator, it is bigger than 1/2. If less, it is smaller. For 3/7: 3 is less than half of 7 (3.5), so 3/7 < 1/2.

quiz.q: Which is bigger: 3/5 or 2/5?
quiz.explanation: Same denominator (5). Compare numerators: 3 > 2, so 3/5 > 2/5.

quiz.q: Which is bigger: 1/3 or 1/8?
quiz.explanation: Same numerator (1). Smaller denominator (3) means bigger pieces, so 1/3 > 1/8.

quiz.q: Is 3/6 greater than, less than, or equal to 1/2?
quiz.explanation: 3/6 = 1/2 because 3 is exactly half of 6. They are equivalent!

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions with Like Denominators
lessons.description: Add and subtract fractions that have the same denominator — just add or subtract the numerators!
lessons.formula:
Like denominator rule:
a/c + b/c = (a+b)/c
a/c - b/c = (a-b)/c

The denominator stays the SAME. Only the numerators change!
Example: 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5.
lessons.content:
When fractions have the same denominator, adding and subtracting them is surprisingly simple! The denominator tells you the size of each piece. If you're working with fifths, every piece is the same size — one-fifth of a whole. So when you add fifths together, the pieces don't change size; you just get more of them. For example, 1/5 of a pizza plus 2/5 of a pizza equals 3/5 of a pizza. You only combine the top numbers (numerators): 1 + 2 = 3.

Here's the key rule: keep the denominator the same and only add or subtract the numerators. So 2/8 + 3/8 = (2+3)/8 = 5/8. Think of it like counting pieces of the same size. If you have 2 slices of an 8-slice pizza and someone gives you 3 more slices of the same pizza, you now have 5 slices total — still out of 8. Subtraction works the same way: 7/10 - 4/10 = 3/10. You had 7 tenths, took away 4 tenths, and 3 tenths remain.

A common mistake is adding the denominators too, like writing 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/6. That's wrong! Remember: the denominator is just the name of the piece size. One third plus one third is two thirds (2/3), not two sixths. Another tip: always check if your answer can be simplified. For example, 2/8 + 2/8 = 4/8, which simplifies to 1/2. But simplifying is a separate step — first, just add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator.
steps: Check that both fractions have the same denominator
Keep the common denominator unchanged
Add (or subtract) only the numerators
Write the result as a single fraction with the same denominator
Check if the answer can be simplified to lowest terms

examples.title: Adding Like Fractions
examples.text: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8. The denominator 8 stays the same. We add only the numerators: 2 + 3 = 5. Think of it as 2 slices plus 3 slices of the same pizza — you get 5 slices out of 8.

examples.title: Subtracting Like Fractions
examples.text: 7/10 - 4/10 = 3/10. Both fractions are tenths, so the denominator stays 10. Subtract only the numerators: 7 - 4 = 3. You started with 7 tenths, took away 4 tenths, and 3 tenths remain.

lessons.tip: Think of pizza slices! If each fraction is a slice from the same pizza (same denominator), just count your total slices — don't change the pizza size!

quiz.explanation: Keep the denominator 5, add the numerators: 1 + 2 = 3. So 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5.
Keep the denominator 6, subtract the numerators: 5 - 2 = 3. So 5/6 - 2/6 = 3/6 (which simplifies to 1/2).

quiz.q: Which rule is correct for adding fractions with like denominators?
options: Add numerators only, keep the denominator
quiz.explanation: When denominators are the same, add only the numerators and keep the common denominator unchanged.
Keep denominator 9, add numerators: 3 + 4 = 7. So 3/9 + 4/9 = 7/9.

lessons.title: Area & Perimeter
lessons.description: Calculate the area and perimeter of rectangles and related shapes!
lessons.formula:
Area of a rectangle:
A = length × width
Perimeter of a rectangle:
P = 2 × (length + width)
or P = l + l + w + w
lessons.content:
Area is the amount of space inside a shape, measured in square units. Think of it like how many 1×1 squares would fit inside. Perimeter is the distance around the outside of a shape — like walking around the edges.

For a rectangle with length 5 and width 3: Area = 5 × 3 = 15 square units. Perimeter = 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 units (or 2 × (5+3) = 16).

Squares are special rectangles where all sides are equal. For a square with side 4: Area = 4 × 4 = 16 sq units. Perimeter = 4 × 4 = 16 units. The area and perimeter happen to be the same number here, but they measure different things!
steps: For area: identify length and width of the rectangle
Multiply length × width to get area in square units
For perimeter: add all four sides together
Or use the formula: P = 2 × (length + width)
Always include units: square units for area, regular units for perimeter

examples.title: Area of a Garden
examples.text: A rectangular garden is 8 m long and 5 m wide. Area = 8 × 5 = 40 square meters. Perimeter = 2 × (8 + 5) = 26 meters.

examples.title: Comparing Rooms
examples.text: Room A: 6 ft × 4 ft. Area = 24 sq ft. Room B: 7 ft × 3 ft. Area = 21 sq ft. Room A has more floor space!

lessons.tip: Area is INSIDE (multiply — like filling up), perimeter is OUTSIDE (add — like fencing around). Remember: Area = All squares inside, Perimeter = Path around the edges!

quiz.q: What is the area of a 6 by 4 rectangle?
quiz.explanation: Area = length × width = 6 × 4 = 24 square units.

quiz.q: What is the perimeter of a 5 by 3 rectangle?
quiz.explanation: Perimeter = 2 × (5 + 3) = 2 × 8 = 16 units.

quiz.q: A square has a side of 7 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explanation: Area of a square = side × side = 7 × 7 = 49 sq cm.

quiz.q: Which measures the OUTSIDE of a shape?
quiz.explanation: Perimeter measures the distance around the outside of a shape.

lessons.title: Angles & Polygons
lessons.description: Identify angle types and classify polygons by their properties!
lessons.formula:
Angle Types:
Acute: less than 90°
Right: exactly 90°
Obtuse: more than 90° (but less than 180°)
Polygon Names:
3 = triangle, 5 = pentagon, 6 = hexagon
lessons.content:
An angle is formed where two lines meet at a point called the vertex. Angles come in different sizes. An acute angle is small (less than 90°), a right angle is exactly 90° (like the corner of a square), and an obtuse angle is big (more than 90° but less than 180°).

Polygons are closed shapes with straight sides. They're named by the number of sides: triangle (3), quadrilateral (4), pentagon (5), hexagon (6). A regular polygon has all sides and angles equal!

You can find angles everywhere — the corner of a book is a right angle, a slice of pizza forms an acute angle, and a partially opened door makes an obtuse angle.
steps: Look at where two lines meet to find an angle
Compare to a right angle (90°) to classify: smaller = acute, bigger = obtuse
Count sides to name a polygon
Look for right angles using a square corner test
Regular polygons have all equal sides and angles

examples.title: Classifying Angles
examples.text: A door slightly open makes an acute angle. A door fully open (perpendicular to wall) makes a 90° right angle. A door opened wider makes an obtuse angle.

examples.title: Naming Polygons
examples.text: A stop sign has 8 sides = octagon. A honeycomb cell has 6 sides = hexagon. The Pentagon building has 5 sides = pentagon.

lessons.tip: Use the corner of a piece of paper to test for right angles! Hold the corner of the paper at the vertex — if the sides of the angle match the paper's corner, it's a right angle (90°).

quiz.q: An angle less than 90° is called:
quiz.explanation: Acute angles are smaller than 90°, like a sharp point.

quiz.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?
quiz.explanation: 'Hex' means six. A hexagon has 6 sides.

quiz.q: Which angle is exactly 90°?
quiz.explanation: A right angle is exactly 90° — the corner of a square.

quiz.q: A pentagon has how many sides?
quiz.explanation: 'Penta' means five. A pentagon has 5 sides.

lessons.title: Mass and Capacity
lessons.description: Measure and estimate mass in grams and kilograms and capacity in liters and milliliters.
lessons.formula:
Mass Units:
1 kilogram (kg) = 1,000 grams (g)
A book ~ 300 g,  A cat ~ 4 kg

Capacity Units:
1 liter (L) = 1,000 milliliters (mL)
A glass of water ~ 250 mL
A large bottle ~ 2 L
lessons.content:
Mass is how heavy something is, and we measure it in grams (g) and kilograms (kg). A gram is very light — a paperclip weighs about 1 gram. A kilogram is 1,000 grams — a typical watermelon weighs about 2 kilograms. We use a scale to measure mass.

Capacity is how much liquid a container can hold, measured in liters (L) and milliliters (mL). A small juice box holds about 200 mL, while a large milk jug holds about 2 L. We use measuring cups and beakers to measure capacity. Estimating before you measure helps build your number sense!
steps: Decide if the item is heavy or light to choose grams or kilograms
For mass: place the object on a scale and read the measurement
For capacity: use a measuring cup or beaker and read the markings
Estimate first, then measure to see how close your estimate was
Convert if needed: 1 kg = 1,000 g and 1 L = 1,000 mL

examples.title: Estimating Mass
examples.text: A pineapple weighs about 1 kg. A pencil weighs about 5 g. An elephant weighs about 5,000 kg. Which unit would you use for a backpack? Kilograms (about 3 kg).

examples.title: Measuring Capacity
examples.text: A teapot holds about 1 L of water. A teaspoon holds about 5 mL. A bathtub holds about 150 L. To measure 500 mL of milk, you could use a measuring cup.

lessons.tip: A good rule of thumb: if you can easily hold it in one hand, measure in grams or milliliters. If it takes two hands or is very large, use kilograms or liters. Think about real objects to help you estimate!

quiz.q: Which unit would you use to measure the mass of a dog?
quiz.explanation: A dog is heavy, so we use kilograms. A typical dog might weigh 15 kg.

quiz.q: How many grams are in 3 kilograms?
A water bottle holds 500 mL. How many bottles to make 1 liter?

lessons.title: Elapsed Time
lessons.description: Calculate how much time passes between two events using number lines and clocks.
lessons.formula:
Elapsed Time:
Start: 3:15  →  End: 4:45

On a number line:
3:15 → 3:30 = 15 min
3:30 → 4:00 = 30 min
4:00 → 4:45 = 45 min
Total = 15 + 30 + 45 = 90 min = 1 hr 30 min
lessons.content:
Elapsed time is the amount of time that passes from a start time to an end time. For example, if a movie starts at 2:00 PM and ends at 3:30 PM, the elapsed time is 1 hour and 30 minutes. A time number line is a great tool: draw a line, mark the start time on the left and the end time on the right, then jump to friendly times (like the next hour) to count the minutes.

To find elapsed time, you can count forward from the start or backward from the end. Break the time into chunks: first count minutes to the next hour, then count full hours, then count the remaining minutes. Add all the chunks together to get the total elapsed time.
steps: Identify the start time and end time
Draw a number line and mark the start time on the left
Jump to the next hour and count those minutes
Jump through any full hours (each = 60 minutes)
Jump from the last full hour to the end time and add remaining minutes
Add all the jumps together to find total elapsed time

examples.title: School to Dinner
examples.text: School ends at 3:15 PM. Dinner is at 6:00 PM. Jump: 3:15→4:00 (45 min), 4:00→5:00 (60 min), 5:00→6:00 (60 min). Total: 45 + 60 + 60 = 165 min = 2 hr 45 min.

examples.title: Soccer Practice
examples.text: Practice starts at 10:00 AM and lasts 1 hour and 30 minutes. End time: 10:00 + 1:30 = 11:30 AM.

lessons.tip: When finding elapsed time across noon or midnight, remember: 11:59 AM becomes 12:00 PM (noon), and 11:59 PM becomes 12:00 AM (midnight). The hours keep going — only the AM/PM changes!

quiz.q: A movie starts at 2:15 PM and ends at 4:00 PM. How long is the movie?
You start homework at 5:30 PM and finish at 6:15 PM. How long did it take?
A bus ride takes 35 minutes. If it leaves at 8:20 AM, when does it arrive?

lessons.title: Area Models
lessons.description: Use rectangular arrays and area models to understand multiplication.
lessons.formula:
Area of a Rectangle:
Area = length x width

Array: 4 rows x 5 columns = 20 squares
Area = 4 x 5 = 20 square units

The array IS the area model!
lessons.content:
An area model is a rectangle where the length and width represent the two factors in a multiplication problem. The area inside the rectangle equals the product. For 4 x 5, you draw a rectangle that is 4 units long and 5 units wide, then count all the squares inside: 20 squares total.

Area models connect multiplication to geometry. The word area means the total space inside a shape. When you draw a 3-by-6 array, you can see that 3 x 6 = 18 because there are 18 unit squares. This visual approach helps you understand WHY multiplication works, not just memorize the answers.
steps: Identify the two factors (the numbers being multiplied)
Draw a rectangle with the first factor as the number of rows
Make the second factor the number of columns
Count all the unit squares inside the rectangle
Write the equation: rows x columns = area (product)

examples.title: Area Model for 6 x 7
examples.text: Draw a rectangle with 6 rows and 7 columns. Count the squares: 42 total. So 6 x 7 = 42 square units. The area model proves it!

examples.title: Array for 3 x 9
examples.text: Draw 3 rows of 9 dots each. Count: 9 + 9 + 9 = 27. The rectangular array has 27 unit squares. 3 x 9 = 27.

lessons.tip: Area models are especially helpful for larger multiplication problems later! In 4th and 5th grade, you will break big problems like 23 x 15 into smaller rectangles using the area model. Getting comfortable now makes future math much easier!

quiz.q: What is the area of a rectangle that is 5 rows by 8 columns?
quiz.explanation: Area = 5 x 8 = 40 square units.

quiz.q: An area model has 7 rows and 6 columns. What multiplication fact does it show?
quiz.explanation: Rows x columns = 7 x 6 = 42 square units.

quiz.q: If an area model shows 36 squares with 9 columns, how many rows?
quiz.explanation: 9 x ? = 36. Since 9 x 4 = 36, there are 4 rows.

lessons.title: Data & Probability Basics
lessons.description: Collect, organize, and interpret data. Explore basic probability!
lessons.formula:
Probability = how likely something is:
Certain (100%) — always happens
Likely — probably happens
Unlikely — probably won't
Impossible (0%) — can't happen
lessons.content:
Data is collected information. You can show data using bar graphs, pictographs (pictures instead of bars), and line plots (X marks on a number line). Each type has strengths for showing different kinds of data.

Probability is the chance that something will happen. Something certain always happens (the sun will rise). Something impossible never happens (pigs will fly). Many events fall between — likely or unlikely.

When you flip a coin, it's equally likely to land on heads or tails — that's a 50/50 chance! Understanding probability helps you make predictions about events.
steps: Collect data by surveying, counting, or measuring
Organize data in a table or tally chart
Choose the best graph type for your data
Read graphs by looking at labels, scales, and bar heights
Describe probability using certain, likely, unlikely, or impossible

examples.title: Reading a Pictograph
examples.text: A pictograph shows favorite sports with basketball ⛹ = 4 votes. If basketball shows 3 symbols, that's 3 × 4 = 12 votes.

examples.title: Probability Examples
examples.text: Rolling a die: getting 1-6 is certain (all outcomes). Rolling a 7 is impossible (not on die). Rolling an even number is likely (3 out of 6).

lessons.tip: When creating graphs, ALWAYS include a title and labels! Without labels, nobody knows what the graph shows. Also make sure your scale is consistent — if one bar represents 2 votes, all bars should use the same scale.

quiz.q: What is the probability of rolling a 7 on a standard die?
quiz.explanation: A standard die has numbers 1-6. There's no 7, so it's impossible!

quiz.q: On a pictograph, if each symbol represents 3 students and there are 4 symbols for soccer, how many chose soccer?
quiz.explanation: 4 symbols × 3 students each = 12 students chose soccer.

quiz.q: Which event is CERTAIN?
quiz.explanation: A week always has 7 days — that's 100% certain!

quiz.q: What is the probability of flipping heads on a fair coin?
quiz.explanation: A fair coin has a 50/50 chance — equally likely heads or tails.

lessons.title: Introduction to Variables
lessons.description: Use letters and symbols to represent unknown quantities in simple equations.
lessons.formula:
Variables in Equations:
n + 5 = 12  →  n = 7
(the unknown n equals 7)

To solve: do the opposite operation
12 - 5 = 7, so n = 7

? x 4 = 24  →  ? = 6
24 ÷ 4 = 6
lessons.content:
A variable is a letter or symbol that stands for an unknown number. When you see an equation like n + 5 = 12, the letter n is the variable. Your job is to figure out what number n represents. Think of an equation as a balance scale: both sides must be equal.

To find the value of the variable, use the inverse operation (the opposite). If the equation adds 5, you subtract 5 to solve it. If it multiplies by 4, you divide by 4. This is the beginning of algebra, and you are learning it in 3rd grade!
steps: Read the equation and find the variable (the letter or symbol)
Identify what operation is being done to the variable
Use the inverse (opposite) operation to isolate the variable
Check: put your answer back into the equation to verify it works
If both sides are equal, you found the correct value

examples.title: Solving n + 8 = 15
examples.text: The equation adds 8 to n. Use the inverse: subtract 8 from 15. 15 - 8 = 7. So n = 7. Check: 7 + 8 = 15. Correct!

examples.title: Solving ? x 3 = 18
examples.text: The equation multiplies ? by 3. Use the inverse: divide 18 by 3. 18 ÷ 3 = 6. So ? = 6. Check: 6 x 3 = 18. Correct!

lessons.tip: Think of equations like a balance scale. If you have 3 + n on one side and 10 on the other, the scale is balanced when n = 7. Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other to keep it balanced!

quiz.q: Solve: n + 7 = 14. What is n?
Solve: m - 4 = 9. What is m?
Solve: k x 5 = 30. What is k?

lessons.title: Multi-Step Word Problems
lessons.description: Solve 2-step word problems using addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
lessons.formula:
Two-Step Problem Strategy:
Step 1: Read and find the first question
Step 2: Solve Step 1
Step 3: Use the answer from Step 1 in Step 2
Step 4: Solve Step 2 for the final answer

Example: 3 bags of 4 apples. Eat 5. How many left?
Step 1: 3 x 4 = 12 apples
Step 2: 12 - 5 = 7 apples left
lessons.content:
Multi-step word problems require more than one operation to solve. Instead of a single addition or multiplication, you need to do two or more steps. For example: 'Emma buys 3 packs of stickers with 8 stickers each. She gives 10 to her friend. How many does she have left?' First multiply (3 x 8 = 24), then subtract (24 - 10 = 14).

The key to multi-step problems is breaking them into smaller pieces. Read the problem carefully, decide what to do first, solve that part, then use that answer for the next step. Drawing a picture or writing an equation for each step helps you stay organized.
steps: Read the entire problem at least twice
Ask: what do I need to find first? (first step)
Solve the first step and write down the answer
Ask: what do I do next with this answer? (second step)
Solve the second step to get the final answer
Check: does your final answer make sense in the original story?

examples.title: Sticker Problem
examples.text: Maya buys 4 boxes of crayons with 6 crayons each. She gives 8 crayons to her brother. How many crayons does Maya have left? Step 1: 4 x 6 = 24 crayons. Step 2: 24 - 8 = 16 crayons left.

examples.title: Classroom Seating
examples.text: There are 5 tables with 4 chairs each. 3 chairs are broken. How many good chairs? Step 1: 5 x 4 = 20 total chairs. Step 2: 20 - 3 = 17 good chairs.

lessons.tip: Circle the numbers AND the operation words in the problem. Words like 'each' and 'groups of' often mean multiply. Words like 'left' and 'remaining' often mean subtract. Underlining these clues helps you plan your steps!

quiz.q: A baker makes 5 trays of 6 cookies. He sells 12. How many are left?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: 5 x 6 = 30 cookies. Step 2: 30 - 12 = 18 cookies left.

quiz.q: There are 4 rows of 7 desks. 3 students move to another class. How many desks are still occupied?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: 4 x 7 = 28 desks. Step 2: 28 - 3 = 25 desks still occupied.

quiz.q: A garden has 3 sections with 8 plants each. 5 plants die. How many live plants?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: 3 x 8 = 24 plants. Step 2: 24 - 5 = 19 live plants.
